Dear Imran,

Thank you for the lovely lunch last Sunday. Your daughter and I have been talking about how to make our visits easier for everyone, because with our shifts we often arrive tired and hurried. Could we try something for two months? We would come on the first and third Sundays and stay properly, with our phones put away. At the end of the two months the three of us can sit down and say what worked and what did not, and change it if it isn't right. It is only an experiment, not a new rule, and you are very welcome to suggest changes now. We love these lunches and want to keep them good.

With warm regards,
Tushar 🙂

qa.q: On which Sundays did Tushar suggest coming for lunch?
qa.a: On the first and third Sundays.

qa.q: What does Tushar hope Imran will feel about the proposal?
qa.a: Tushar hopes Imran will feel reassured that this is not a rejection, since the letter calls it "only an experiment, not a new rule".

qa.q: What could Tushar and Imran's daughter do if the trial turns out to be too few visits?
qa.a: At the end of the two months they could add a lunch or a short evening visit, because a trial can be adjusted without anyone losing face.

qa.q: How might Imran read the letter?
qa.a: Imran may feel valued at being asked and invited to suggest changes, though there could be a little sadness about fewer lunches.

grounding: Tushar proposes a small two-month trial of lunches rather than a permanent rule.

Ojas, you asked how we sorted out the Sunday lunch war with my parents. I'm Chetan, and I'll be honest, I nearly made it worse.
My parents wanted us every Sunday. My wife, Pallavi, was burning out after her night shifts. My first idea was to announce, "From now on, twice a month." Final. Rule.
Pallavi stopped me. She said, "That sounds like we're rejecting them forever. What if we call it a trial?"
So that's what we told them. "For the next two months, let's try lunch twice a month and see how it feels for everyone. Then we'll talk again."
My mother frowned, but she agreed. A trial is easy to agree to.
Two months later, she said, "Actually, twice a month is nice. I get more time to plan the menu." We kept it.

qa.q: How often did Chetan's family try lunch during the trial?
What did Chetan's mother's frown show about how she felt when the trial was suggested?
qa.a: It showed she was unhappy and a little hurt at fewer lunches, but willing to accept it because it was only a trial.

qa.q: What else could Chetan and Pallavi have done if the trial didn't work for the parents?
qa.a: They could talk again at the end of two months, hear what felt hard, and adjust the arrangement together.

qa.q: How did the arrangement look to Chetan's mother after two months?
qa.a: She found she liked it, since twice a month gave her more time to plan the menu.

grounding: It shows a couple proposing a two-month trial of lunches twice a month instead of a permanent rule, which feels less like rejection and is easier to accept.

I live in the flat above Madhav's parents in Kochi, so I hear the Sunday lunches through the floor.
For a while they'd been tense. Madhav and his wife, Leena, came every Sunday, and lately there were raised voices about it. Leena works Saturday shifts at the hospital; I think she was worn out.
Then one Sunday in March I heard Madhav say, "Appa, Amma, can we try something? For two months, let's do lunch twice a month. Then we'll all see how it feels."
His father said, "And if we don't like it?"
"Then we talk and change it."
A pause. Then his mother laughed. "Two months, fine. But I'm making biryani on those two days."
I don't know what they all thought privately. But the voices downstairs got softer. By May, I heard Leena laughing in the kitchen with Madhav's mother.
— Jomon

qa.a: In the flat above Madhav's parents in Kochi.

qa.q: What might Madhav's mother have been feeling when she laughed and agreed?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved that it was only a trial, and willing to try because it didn't feel like a permanent rejection.

qa.q: What else could Madhav do to make the trial succeed?
qa.a: He could plan a calm talk with his parents at the end of the two months to hear what worked and what didn't.

qa.q: How does the change seem to affect Leena, as far as Jomon can tell?
qa.a: Leena seems happier and more relaxed, since by May she is laughing in the kitchen with Madhav's mother.

grounding: It shows, through a neighbour's account, a couple proposing a two-month trial of fewer lunches rather than a permanent rule, which the family accepts more easily.
